notes: Shared tokenizer contract (docs/stage3-contracts.md §1). Python: content/tools/tokenizer.py; Swift: SharedKernel/TextTokenizer.swift. Both must reproduce every case.
tokens[].w is the original text slice, ch = [start, end) in Unicode code points (Python len), n = normalized form, present only when it differs from w.
Normalized: lowercase; apostrophes ’ ‘ ` ʼ → '; hyphens ‐ ‑ → -; soft hyphen U+00AD removed.
A word starts at a letter or number (Unicode L*, N*) and continues over letters, numbers and combining marks (M*).
Joiners stay inside a word only between two letters/numbers: apostrophes (don't, Uber’s, rock'n'roll), hyphens (AI-powered, day-to-day, 10-3, 555-0100), soft hyphen.
Leading/trailing apostrophes and hyphens are not part of the word: 'Tis → Tis, students' → students, two- → two.
Between two digits . and , join: 3.5, 1,000, 2.0.1, 1.5k. Spelling numbers out is the G2P/scorer's job, not the tokenizer's.
Dots between letters split: U.S. → U, S; e.g. → e, g; a.m. → a, m. Content agent should expand such abbreviations in sentences meant for reading aloud.
En/em dashes, slashes, colons, %, $, #, +, ×, @, _ and all other symbols split: 10–20 → 10, 20; 24/7 → 24, 7; 9:30 → 9, 30; URLs split into parts.
Emoji and other symbols (S*) are skipped; non-Latin letters (Cyrillic, CJK) are words; superscripts/fractions (No) are numbers: x², ½.

How to handle uncertainty with AI vendors and disaster recovery (DR) approaches to consider.
An excerpt from the book Building Resilient Distributed Systems by Sam Newman.
Last week’s guest on the podcast was Sam Newman, who had released a book I’ve personally long awaited titled Building Resilient Distributed Systems.
I asked Sam if he would consider sharing an excerpt from the book, with sections especially relevant for anyone building systems that ought to be reliable.
Sam graciously agreed, and today’s issue covers a few important topics, spread across two chapters from his book.
My usual disclaimer: as with all my recommendations, I was not paid to recommend this book, and none of the links are affiliate ones.
But what happens when a catastrophic failure causes widespread outage of large parts of your system?

Fire, flood, electrical supply issues, and errors in the underlying cloud infrastructure are all outside of your control, and at one fell swoop, they can render your attempts to make your system more robust totally redundant.
Handling these situations falls under the auspices of disaster recovery (DR), a set of procedures that should kick in when something really bad happens.
As with much of what we’ve looked at in this book, trade-offs abound.
When running on a private cloud or in a more traditional on-premises setup, you’ll instead think in terms of data centers.

So when deciding on the appropriate RPO and RTO, there needs to be a discussion with stakeholders regarding end-user needs and regulatory and legislative requirements, which are balanced against the cost and complexity of implementing the required solution.

For example, a backup and restore approach requires rerouting, a pilot light setup will add the need for cross-site data replication and infrastructure automation, and a warm failover adds on the cost of having some infrastructure ready to go.
Note that they all require some form of rerouting of traffic, and most require some form of cross-site data replication.

Ideally, your failover site runs the same core technology stack as the primary site, meaning that any investment in infrastructure automation on your primary can also be used on the failover (for example, being able to reuse Terraform scripts).
A caveat to spinning up infrastructure on demand here comes in terms of guaranteeing that infrastructure is actually available when you need it, something we’ll explore later in this chapter.

Cold, Warm, and Hot Failovers: A brief note is warranted here regarding the term warm.

You’ll find various solutions and vendor products promising cold, warm, or hot failover, with the only real distinguishing factor between these terms often being that a hot failover would give you a lower RTO in comparison to a warm failover, and a warm failover would give you a lower RTO than a cold one.

In a scenario where a major cloud vendor’s region has failed, you may find yourself fighting over scraps with everyone else.
A solution here is to consider ensuring that your software can still operate even if the model is unavailable.

When using backup vendors like this, there may be a lag in terms of how quickly the latest models may be available, but given that you may not always want to be on the bleeding edge of the models you use to embed in your software (something we’ll discuss in just a moment), this is probably fine.
I’ve seen reports where a model has started behaving differently, without any major change in behavior being flagged by the vendor.

It is therefore vital to have a good set of tests to validate that the AI portions of your code are behaving appropriately—and this should be a mix of traditional functional tests, together with the use of AI evaluation tools (evals).
If Cursor had been able to use AI models from another firm, it might have been less vulnerable to this issue.
Keep Your Options Open: Make sure you aren’t wholly dependent on a single model or AI platform.

In his 2025 talk at LeadDev Berlin, “LLMs: An Operator’s View”, Stanier explains that if you see a person spending a lot of money, this shouldn’t be seen as a bad thing, as typically it shows someone trying to get more done.
It can also help you spot egregious overspend.
Uber recently revealed that it had burned through its entire annual AI budget in just the first four months of the year.

It can help you understand how people are using it and also help you spot when the bills start climbing precipitously.

At the macro level, concerns about the AI sector as a whole mean we are dealing with an ever-changing (and hopefully) improving set of products built on very shaky financial foundations.
